A few days later, Virginia and her curly-haired companion went riding in Brockley meadows. While passing through a hedge, she tore her riding dress so badly that, when she returned, she decided to use the back stairs to avoid being seen. As she hurried past the Tapestry Chamber, whose door stood open, she thought she glimpsed someone inside. Supposing it was her mother's maid, who sometimes brought her sewing there, she looked in to ask for help repairing the dress. To her great surprise, the person was the Canterville Ghost himself! He sat beside the window, watching the faded gold of the yellowing trees blow through the air and red leaves whirl wildly along the long avenue. His head rested on his hand, and everything about him suggested deep misery. He looked so lonely and worn out that little Virginia felt sorry for him. Her first thought had been to run away and lock herself in her room, but instead she decided to try to comfort him. Her steps were so quiet, and his sadness so deep, that he did not notice her until she spoke.

“I'm very sorry for you,” she said. “But my brothers are going back to Eton tomorrow. After that, if you behave yourself, nobody will bother you.”

“It's absurd to ask me to behave myself,” he replied, turning in surprise towards the pretty little girl who had dared to speak to him. “Quite absurd. I have to rattle my chains, groan through keyholes, and wander about at night, if that's what you mean. It's my only reason for existing.”

“That is no reason to exist at all. And you know you've been very wicked. On our first day here, Mrs. Umney told us you had killed your wife.”

“Well, I admit that,” the Ghost said crossly, “but it was entirely a family matter and had nothing to do with anyone else.”

“Killing anyone is very wrong,” Virginia said. At times she had a sweet, stern seriousness inherited from some old Puritan ancestor in New England.

“Oh, I hate the easy harshness of moral rules! My wife was very plain, never had my ruffled collars properly starched, and knew nothing about cooking. Why, I once shot a buck in Hogley Woods—a magnificent young deer—and do you know how she had it served at dinner? Still, none of that matters now. It's all over. And although I did kill her, I don't think it was very nice of her brothers to starve me to death.”

He gave a shudder and withdrew, shutting the window after him.

At the door he turned the key and pulled it open. He did not so much as look towards the murdered man. He felt that everything depended upon refusing to grasp the situation. The friend who had painted that fatal portrait, the source of all his misery, had passed out of his life. That sufficed.

Then the lamp occurred to him. It was an unusual piece of Moorish work, fashioned in dull silver with inlaid arabesques of polished steel and rough turquoises set into it. His servant might notice its absence and begin asking questions. For a moment he wavered; then he went back and lifted it from the table. He could not avoid looking at the dead thing. How motionless it lay! How dreadful the whiteness of those long hands! It resembled some terrible figure made of wax.

After locking the door behind him, he stole softly down the stairs. The wood creaked beneath him and seemed to utter cries of pain. More than once he halted and listened. No; all was quiet. He had heard only his own steps.

Reaching the library, he noticed the coat and bag in the corner. Somewhere must be found to conceal them. He unlocked a cupboard hidden in the wainscoting, where he stored his own strange disguises, and placed them inside. They could readily be burnt later. Next he drew out his watch. The time was twenty minutes before two.

He seated himself and began to reflect. Each year—almost every month—men in England were strangled for doing what he had done. A murderous madness had filled the air. Some red star had approached too near the earth.... Yet what proof existed against him? Basil Hallward had gone out at eleven. Nobody had witnessed his return. Most of the servants were away at Selby Royal. His valet had retired.... Paris! Of course. Basil had departed for Paris on the midnight train, exactly as he planned. Given his peculiar, reserved ways, months would pass before anyone suspected anything. Months! Long before that, every trace could be destroyed.

An idea suddenly came to him. He put on his hat and fur coat and stepped into the hall. There he stopped, hearing a policeman's slow, weighty footfall on the pavement outside and catching the reflection of the bull's-eye lamp in the window. He stood waiting, scarcely breathing.

A few moments later he lifted the latch and slipped outside, closing the door with the utmost gentleness. Then he started to ring the bell.

In fact, he was costumed as “Jonas the Graveless, or the Corpse-Snatcher of Chertsey Barn,” one of his most extraordinary roles. The Cantervilles had good reason to remember it, since it had been the true cause of their quarrel with their neighbor, Lord Rufford. It was about a quarter past two in the morning, and as far as he could tell, nobody was awake. But as he wandered towards the library to check whether any trace of the bloodstain remained, two figures suddenly sprang at him from a dark corner, waving their arms wildly overhead and screaming “BOO!” into his ear.

Naturally enough in the circumstances, he panicked and fled towards the stairs, only to find Washington Otis waiting with the large garden syringe. Surrounded by enemies and almost cornered, he disappeared into the great iron stove, which fortunately was unlit. He had to struggle home through the flues and chimneys and reached his own room filthy, disheveled, and utterly despairing.

After this, nobody saw him on another nighttime expedition. The twins ambushed him several times and scattered nutshells along the corridors every night, much to the irritation of their parents and the servants, but nothing worked. Clearly his feelings were too deeply hurt for him to appear. Mr. Otis accordingly returned to his major history of the Democratic Party, a work he had been writing for several years. Mrs. Otis arranged a magnificent clambake that astonished the entire county. The boys occupied themselves with lacrosse, euchre, poker, and other American national games. Virginia rode her pony along the lanes with the young Duke of Cheshire, who had come to spend the last week of his holiday at Canterville Chase. Everyone assumed the ghost had left, and Mr. Otis actually wrote to Lord Canterville saying so. In reply, Lord Canterville expressed his great delight at the news and sent warm congratulations to the Minister's admirable wife.

The Otises were mistaken, however. The ghost remained in the house, and although he was now practically an invalid, he had no intention of letting matters end there. This was especially true after he heard that the young Duke of Cheshire was among the guests. The Duke's great-uncle, Lord Francis Stilton, had once bet Colonel Carbury a hundred guineas that he would play dice with the Canterville ghost. The next morning he had been found on the card-room floor in such a helpless state of paralysis that, although he lived to a very old age, he never again managed to say anything except “Double Sixes.”
